title: Unit 10: Infinite Sequences and Series

topics.name: Convergence and common series
covers: Applying limits to understand convergence of infinite series
Types of series: Geometric, harmonic, and p-series

topics.name: Convergence tests and error bounds
covers: A test for divergence and several tests for convergence
Approximating sums of convergent infinite series and associated error bounds

topics.name: Power series and Taylor series
covers: Determining the radius and interval of convergence for a series
Representing a function as a Taylor series or a Maclaurin series on an appropriate interval

guide.title: Infinite sequences and series: review guide
guide.intro: This BC-only unit asks when an infinite sum has a finite value, how to test it, how far a partial sum can be from the total, and how to write functions as power series.

sections.title: Convergence and common series
body: A series Σaₙ converges if its partial sums Sₙ = a₁ + … + aₙ approach a finite limit; that limit is the sum.

Geometric series Σ arⁿ converge to a/(1 − r) (first term over 1 minus the ratio) when |r| < 1 and diverge otherwise. p-series Σ 1/nᵖ converge for p > 1 and diverge for p ≤ 1; the harmonic series Σ 1/n (p = 1) diverges.
points: The first term matters in a/(1 − r): start counting from the series' actual first term.
Σ 1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2, so it diverges.
A sequence converging is different from its series converging.

sections.title: Convergence tests and error bounds
body: nth-term test: if aₙ doesn't approach 0, the series diverges. (If aₙ → 0, the test says nothing.) Other tests: integral, comparison and limit comparison, alternating series, and ratio (L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|; converges if L < 1, diverges if L > 1, inconclusive if L = 1).

A series converges absolutely if Σ|aₙ| converges, and conditionally if it converges but Σ|aₙ| doesn't. For an alternating series that meets the test's conditions, the error after n terms is at most the first omitted term. The Lagrange error bound for a Taylor polynomial of degree n is M|x − a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)!, where M bounds |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| on the interval.
points: The nth-term test can prove divergence but never convergence.
Use the ratio test for factorials and exponentials.
The alternating series error bound uses the next term after the last one you used.

sections.title: Power series and Taylor series
body: A power series Σ cₙ(x − a)ⁿ converges on an interval centered at a with radius R, which the ratio test usually finds. Check each endpoint separately; it can converge at both, either, or neither.

The Taylor series of f about x = a is Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x − a)ⁿ/n!; a Maclaurin series has a = 0. Know eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n!, sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …, cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …, and 1/(1 − x) = Σ xⁿ for |x| < 1. Build new series by substituting, multiplying, differentiating, or integrating these.
points: Each Taylor coefficient is f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n!; don't forget the factorial.
Substituting −x² into 1/(1 − x) gives 1/(1 + x²) on |x| < 1.
Differentiating or integrating a power series keeps the radius but may change endpoint behavior.

example.prompt: Find the interval of convergence of Σ (from n = 1) xⁿ/(n·2ⁿ).
example.solution: Ratio test: |x|·n/(2(n + 1)) → |x|/2 < 1, so R = 2. At x = 2 the series is Σ 1/n (harmonic), which diverges. At x = −2 it is Σ (−1)ⁿ/n, which converges by the alternating series test. The interval is [−2, 2).

misconceptions: The harmonic series has aₙ → 0 and diverges.
When L = 1 it is inconclusive; use another test.
“The interval of convergence is always open.”
Check each endpoint; it may be included.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the geometric series 6 + 2 + 2/3 + 2/9 + …?
questions.explanation: The first term is 6 and the ratio is 1/3, so the sum is 6/(1 − 1/3) = 9.
choiceExplanations: |r| = 1/3 < 1, so the series converges.
26/3 is only the sum of the first three terms.
4.5 uses 1 + r instead of 1 − r in the denominator.

questions.explanation: Σ 1/n^(3/2) is a p-series with p = 3/2 > 1, so it converges.
choiceExplanations: Σ (1.01)ⁿ is geometric with r = 1.01 > 1, so it diverges.
Σ 1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1, so it diverges.
Σ 1/n is the harmonic series, which diverges.

questions.prompt: What does the nth-term test tell you about Σ n/(2n + 1)?
choices: It converges, because the terms approach a finite number
It diverges, because the terms approach 1/2, not 0
questions.explanation: lim n→∞ n/(2n + 1) = 1/2 ≠ 0, so the series diverges: it keeps adding about 1/2.
choiceExplanations: A series can converge only if its terms approach 0.
The test is inconclusive only when the terms approach 0.
1/2 is the limit of the terms, not the sum; adding about 1/2 forever grows without bound.

questions.prompt: Using the ratio test, what can you conclude about Σ n²/3ⁿ?
choices: It diverges, because the limit of the ratio is 3
It converges, because the limit of the ratio is 1/3
It diverges, because n² grows without bound
The test is inconclusive, because the limit is 1
choiceExplanations: The ratio is inverted: aₙ₊₁/aₙ has 3ⁿ⁺¹ in the denominator.
3ⁿ grows much faster than n², so the terms approach 0.
(n + 1)²/n² → 1, but the factor 1/3 remains.

questions.prompt: The sum S of Σ (from n = 1) (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n² is approximated by its first four terms. What bound does the alternating series error bound give for the error?
questions.explanation: For an alternating series with decreasing terms approaching 0, the error is at most the first omitted term: 1/5² = 1/25.
choiceExplanations: 1/125 cubes n instead of squaring it.
1/16 is the fourth term, the last one used, not the first one left out.
1/5 forgets to square n.

choices: It diverges by the nth-term test
questions.explanation: It converges by the alternating series test (1/n decreases to 0), but Σ |(−1)ⁿ/n| = Σ 1/n diverges. So it converges conditionally.
choiceExplanations: The terms approach 0, so the nth-term test is inconclusive.
Absolute convergence would need Σ 1/n to converge, and it doesn't.
The divergence of Σ 1/n rules out absolute convergence, not convergence.

questions.prompt: Which is the Maclaurin series for eˣ?
questions.explanation: Every derivative of eˣ equals 1 at x = 0, so each coefficient is 1/n!.
choiceExplanations: 1 − x²/2! + … is the series for cos x.
1 + x + x² + … is the series for 1/(1 − x).
x − x³/3! + … is the series for sin x.

choiceExplanations: This forgets to divide f″(1) by 2!.
This drops the sign of f′(1) = −2.
This centers the polynomial at 0 instead of 1.

questions.prompt: What is the interval of convergence of Σ (x − 2)ⁿ/3ⁿ?
questions.explanation: It's geometric with ratio (x − 2)/3, so it converges when |x − 2| < 3: −1 < x < 5. At both endpoints the terms have absolute value 1, so it diverges there.
choiceExplanations: (−3, 3) is centered at 0, but the series is centered at x = 2.
At x = 5 the series is Σ 1, which diverges.
At x = 5 the series is Σ 1 and at x = −1 it is Σ (−1)ⁿ; both diverge.

questions.prompt: What is the interval of convergence of Σ (from n = 1) xⁿ/n?
questions.explanation: The ratio test gives R = 1. At x = 1 the series is Σ 1/n, which diverges. At x = −1 it is Σ (−1)ⁿ/n, which converges by the alternating series test.
choiceExplanations: x = 1 gives the harmonic series, which diverges.
This reverses the endpoints: x = 1 diverges and x = −1 converges.
The endpoint x = −1 is included: Σ (−1)ⁿ/n converges.

questions.prompt: Using the series for 1/(1 − x), what is the Maclaurin series for 1/(1 + x²)?
questions.explanation: Replace x with −x² in 1 + x + x² + …: 1 − x² + x⁴ − x⁶ + …, valid for |x| < 1.
choiceExplanations: This substitutes −x and gives 1/(1 + x).
This is the series for arctan x, the antiderivative of 1/(1 + x²).
This substitutes x², not −x², and gives 1/(1 − x²).

questions.prompt: The second-degree Maclaurin polynomial for eˣ is used to approximate e^0.2. Given that |f‴(x)| ≤ 1.3 on [0, 0.2], what is the Lagrange error bound?
choiceExplanations: 0.0052 divides by 2! instead of 3!.
0.0104 leaves out the 3! in the denominator.
0.0087 uses (0.2)² instead of (0.2)³.
